title: Lucknow Pact and Bengal Implications
subtitle: The 1916 Congress–League scheme reserved 40% of Bengal’s elected Indian council seats for Muslims.
summary: At Lucknow in December 1916, the Indian National Congress and All-India Muslim League adopted a joint constitutional reform scheme. Congress accepted separate electorates, and the scheme stated Muslim representation in Bengal at 40 percent of elected Indian council members; it also provided Hindu weightage in Bengal. A Pakistan Historical Society history argues that this allocation left Bengal’s Muslim majority without a majority among elected Indian members. The same chapter says the regulations under the Government of India Act, 1919, later reduced Muslim representation in Bengal to 30 percent. These figures describe the scheme and the chapter’s account of later implementation.
heroTagline: The agreed seat formula made Bengal’s Muslim majority a minority among elected Indian members, according to the chapter.
whyItMatters: The chapter makes Bengal a central part of the pact’s compromise: it describes Hindu weightage in Bengal and argues that the Muslim majority consequently lost its legislative majority under the agreed formula, with the 1919 regulations reducing Muslim representation further. This is the Pakistan Historical Society history’s interpretation; Hugh F. Owen’s article abstract separately characterizes the negotiations as enabling later cooperation while alienating important Hindu groups in Bengal and Punjab.

claimCitations.claim: At Lucknow in December 1916, Congress and the Muslim League adopted a joint reform scheme; Congress accepted separate electorates.
The scheme stated Muslim representation at 40 percent of Bengal’s elected Indian council members and provided Hindu weightage in Bengal.

A Pakistan Historical Society history argues that the Bengal allocation meant Muslims lost their majority among elected Indian members; it says regulations under the Government of India Act, 1919, later reduced Muslim representation in Bengal to 30 percent.
Hugh F. Owen’s article abstract says negotiations enabled later cooperation and alienated important Hindu groups in Bengal and Punjab; this characterization is based on the abstract only.

historicalDebate: The Pakistan Historical Society history presents the Bengal seat formula as a disproportionate price for Muslim concessions and says later regulations reduced representation further. This is an attributed interpretation. Owen’s article abstract emphasizes both later cooperation and the alienation of important Hindu groups in Bengal and Punjab; the abstract alone does not settle the local effects.
